strengths: The paper asks an important meta-evaluation question: whether ostensibly different LLM benchmarks measure overlapping capabilities.
The proposed use of perplexity patterns on naturally occurring text as a benchmark signature is creative and potentially useful beyond conventional semantic or performance correlations.
The empirical scope is broad, covering many benchmark subtasks and 32 models from several model families and sizes.
Comparisons among semantic-, performance-, and signature-level overlap reveal plausible artifacts associated with benchmark family and answer format.
The manuscript is generally understandable and provides algorithms, model lists, benchmark lists, and some implementation details.
weaknesses: The central analysis is circular and lacks independent validation. Tokens are selected specifically for predicting each benchmark's performance vector across the 32 models, after which signature similarities are computed using perplexities from those same models. Consequently, the reported structure can be induced by supervised feature selection rather than reveal an independently established capability space.

The feature-selection regime is extremely prone to overfitting: roughly 17 million features are screened using only 32 observations, hundreds of thousands of candidates survive the 2% filter, and stepwise AIC typically selects about 30 variables. AIC does not provide adequate protection in this p-greater-than-n multiple-search setting.

The reported leave-one-out result does not resolve this concern. The paper does not state that screening and forward selection are repeated entirely inside each training fold; if signatures were selected using all 32 models, the MAE estimate leaks held-out outcomes. Even properly nested leave-one-out validation would be unstable with only 32 highly dependent model instances. A genuinely held-out set of models is needed.

Many models are closely related variants, so observations are neither independent nor representative. Model size, family, instruction tuning, architecture, and release generation are heavily confounded with both perplexity and benchmark performance. There are no family-held-out tests or controls showing that signatures capture capabilities rather than these factors.

Perplexity is not directly comparable across the heterogeneous tokenizers in the model set. Splitting contexts on whitespace does not ensure that the recorded last token represents the same unit across models, and within-model z-scoring does not eliminate differences in tokenization or vocabulary.

The claim that signature overlap approximates the 'true' overlap is unsupported because there is no external ground truth, synthetic recovery experiment, human capability annotation, or intervention-based validation. Lower within-format effects alone do not establish construct validity.

The semantic baseline is weak and inconsistently described. It concatenates entire question sets and truncates them to an encoder's maximum length, discarding most questions and making results depend on ordering. The main-text definition samples both benchmarks, whereas Algorithm 3 fixes the smaller benchmark and samples only the larger one.

Key robustness analyses are absent, including comparisons with regularized regression or simpler latent-factor baselines, random-label and random-token controls, sensitivity to corpus sample, screening fraction, AIC stopping rule, model composition, and signature size.

Reporting is insufficient for verifying the main claims. Most evidence is presented as heatmaps or aggregated bar plots, with limited numerical tables, confidence intervals, effect definitions, and multiple-comparison treatment. The claimed Mann-Whitney tests are not documented adequately.

There are reproducibility and internal-consistency problems: no code, signatures, performance matrix, or processed data are provided; random seeds and evaluation prompting details are missing; and the stated reduction from approximately 8.45 billion contexts by a factor of 50 should yield about 169 million, not the reported 16.9 million.

The interpretation overreaches the evidence, including claims of mechanistic insight, benchmark validity, competence-performance conflation, and coding being comparatively 'clean.' At present, the results establish exploratory correlations under one heavily supervised construction, not those broader conclusions.

The empirical scope is ambitious, covering 32 models and many benchmark subfields across knowledge, reasoning, coding, mathematics, and instruction following.
The paper identifies a genuine limitation of performance-correlation analyses: benchmark family, response format, model size, and other nuisance factors can dominate apparent benchmark agreement.
The pipeline and intended overlap calculation are described with algorithms, and the use of naturally occurring corpus contexts is an interesting direction that could motivate stronger future work.
weaknesses: The central evaluation is circular and extremely vulnerable to overfitting. For each benchmark, the method searches millions of token features using performance from only 32 models, selects extreme correlations, and then conducts forward AIC selection. The same model collection is subsequently used to calculate signature overlap. With this feature-to-sample ratio, highly correlated features arise under the null. A genuinely independent set of models is needed for signature validation and overlap analysis.

The reported leave-one-model-out result does not establish generalization. The paper does not clearly state that correlation screening and AIC feature selection are repeated entirely inside every training fold; if features are selected before holding out a model, the MAE estimate leaks test information. Even nested leave-one-out validation would have high variance with 32 related models, yet only aggregate MAEs of 0.075 and 0.180 are reported, without uncertainty, per-benchmark results, or competitive regularized baselines.

The method does not control for general model capability, parameter count, training compute, model family, base-versus-instruction tuning, or release generation. Both corpus perplexity and benchmark accuracy strongly track these variables, so the selected tokens may simply identify generally stronger models rather than benchmark-specific capacities. Multiple variants from the same families also make the 32 observations non-independent. The claim that signatures isolate underlying abilities is therefore unsupported.

The appeal to Sure Independence Screening is not technically justified. Its guarantees require conditions such as adequate signal strength and covariance constraints; the appendix merely asserts that these are plausible. A correlation distribution concentrated near zero with extreme tails is expected when testing millions of null features and is not evidence of sparsity or true signal. No permutation test, false-discovery analysis, stability-selection result, or null simulation is provided.

Perplexities are not directly comparable across the heterogeneous tokenizers and vocabularies used by the 32 models. A whitespace piece can correspond to different token sequences, and recording each model's 'last token' may measure different subword events. Per-model z-scoring does not resolve this semantic mismatch. The exact handling of chat templates, BOS tokens, token aggregation, and base versus instruction-tuned models is also insufficiently specified.

The semantic baseline is weak and arguably invalid. It concatenates benchmark questions, truncates the concatenation to the encoder's maximum length, and embeds that prefix. Consequently, similarity can depend on item ordering and may ignore nearly all questions. This is not a credible set-level semantic-overlap estimator, so outperforming it provides little support for the proposed method.

The statistical analyses treat many pairwise benchmark correlations as independent even though pairs share benchmarks, models, benchmark families, and sometimes aggregate/component scores. Mann-Whitney tests therefore have questionable calibration. Error bars are undefined, multiple-comparison handling is absent, and non-significant family/format differences do not demonstrate that the signature recovers 'true overlap.'

Important robustness and interpretability evidence is missing: there are no examples of selected token contexts, no stability analysis across corpus samples or random seeds, no sensitivity study for the 1% threshold or AIC stopping rule, no independent corpus replication, and no comparison of token/chunk/document representations on held-out predictive validity. Table 1 compares only dispersion and tail magnitude, which does not show that token-level features are more meaningful.

The experimental description contains serious reproducibility inconsistencies. A stated 1-billion-token corpus allegedly yields 8.45 billion whitespace contexts, and downsampling 8.45 billion by 1/50 would produce about 169 million rather than the reported 16.9 million. The exact set/count of the claimed 88 benchmarks is also unclear, and neither code, performance matrices, signatures, nor selected contexts are supplied.

Several conclusions substantially exceed the evidence, including that signatures approximate 'true overlap,' filter out error while preserving systematic ability relations, provide mechanistic insight, establish that coding benchmarks are comparatively clean, or reveal an underlying capacity space. At present the heatmaps are compatible with confounding, selection artifacts, and noise. The idea is interesting, but the central empirical claims are not reliable enough for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper introduces an original and potentially useful perspective: characterizing benchmark relationships through model perplexities on naturally occurring text rather than relying only on question embeddings or raw performance correlations.
The empirical scope is substantial, covering 32 diverse language models, 88 benchmark targets, and a large sample of RedPajama contexts.
The observation that performance correlations can be dominated by benchmark family and answer format is important for benchmark meta-evaluation.
The paper is generally well motivated, and the three-level comparison among semantic, performance, and signature overlap provides a clear organizing framework.
weaknesses: The central analysis is highly vulnerable to selection leakage and overfitting. Signatures are selected from millions of candidate features using performance from only 32 models, and signature similarities are then computed on those same models. It is unclear whether feature screening and selection are repeated inside each leave-one-out fold; otherwise the reported cross-validation error is also optimistic.

With roughly 17 million features and 32 observations, extreme sample correlations will arise abundantly by chance. AIC forward selection after screening does not adequately control this multiple-selection problem. The paper provides no permutation/null experiment showing that equally predictive and structured signatures cannot be obtained from randomized benchmark scores.

The claimed SIS justification is largely qualitative. Its required signal, dependence, and sampling assumptions are not established, while the 32 observations are strongly dependent because many models belong to the same families or checkpoints. Thus, the cited sure-screening guarantees do not directly support this setting.

Construct validity remains insufficiently demonstrated. Correlated average perplexities over outcome-selected tokens do not by themselves establish shared capabilities, and the paper has no controlled benchmarks with known overlap, external capability annotations, or independent model panel against which signature overlap is validated.

The semantic baseline is seriously flawed: questions are concatenated and truncated to the embedding model's context limit, so the result can depend mostly on the first few questions. Moreover, the mathematical definition samples both benchmarks, whereas Algorithm 3 fixes the smaller benchmark and samples only the larger one. This weak baseline does not support claims of superior discrimination.

Several important robustness analyses are absent, including independent corpus samples, alternative screening thresholds and selection methods, repeated seeds, held-out model families, tokenizer effects, and comparisons with factor analysis, partial correlations controlling for model scale/family, IRT-style methods, or improved semantic pooling.

The statistical tests appear to treat many pairwise benchmark correlations as independent even though pairs share benchmarks, which can substantially understate uncertainty. Confidence intervals for the principal overlap estimates and corrections for multiple comparisons are also missing.

Functional coverage is highly imbalanced: most targets are MMLU and BBH subtasks, whereas coding and instruction following appear to be represented by single benchmark families. Broad conclusions such as coding being the cleanest or least entangled capability are therefore weakly supported.

Reproducibility is limited by missing evaluation configurations, prompts, seeds, detailed normalization procedures, selected signatures, and executable code or released artifacts. The precise reference set used for within-model z-scoring is also unclear.

Overall, the idea and scale are promising, but the current evidence does not establish that the reported signature structure reflects benchmark capabilities rather than high-dimensional selection artifacts and model-family confounding. These issues affect the paper's central claims and place it below the top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: identifying redundancy and capability overlap across the rapidly expanding LLM benchmark ecosystem.
The proposed use of perplexity patterns on natural corpora as benchmark signatures is creative and potentially useful as an exploratory meta-evaluation tool.
The empirical scope is substantial, covering many benchmark subtasks and 32 models from several model families.
The appendix includes useful sensitivity analyses across corpora, screening thresholds, feature-selection methods, and nominally held-out models.
weaknesses: The central analysis has severe selection bias. Millions of token features are screened and forward-selected using performance from only 32 models, after which signature overlap is computed using those same models and perplexities. Ordinary AIC does not correct for this massive adaptive search, so apparently strong signatures and correlations can arise from overfitting and winner's curse.

The reported validation does not adequately resolve this concern. It is unclear whether feature screening and selection are repeated strictly within every LOOCV fold; if signatures are selected once using all models, the test labels leak into validation. The separate held-out experiment covers only two models, and the cross-task 'task-specific baseline' appears to measure in-sample fit rather than comparable out-of-sample prediction.

Per-token perplexity is not directly comparable across models with different tokenizers. The manuscript does not precisely explain how a shared whitespace-delimited target is mapped to model-specific subtokens, while using only the last token may measure different strings across models. Within-model z-scoring does not remove this semantic and tokenization confound.

The model sample is highly structured rather than independent: it contains multiple sizes and variants from the same families, mixtures of base and instruction-tuned models, and large capability differences. Architecture, tokenizer, scale, and post-training could jointly drive both perplexity and benchmark scores. These confounds are not controlled, so the signatures cannot be confidently interpreted as specific capability demands.

The semantic-overlap baseline is weak and arguably invalid. It concatenates many questions and truncates the result to the embedding model's maximum length, meaning that most items may never affect the embedding. Only the larger benchmark is resampled in the stated algorithm. Consequently, the claimed superiority over semantic overlap is not convincing.

There is no independent ground truth for benchmark overlap. Broad human-assigned categories are treated as validation when convenient, while counterintuitive results are explained post hoc. Controlled synthetic tasks with known capability mixtures, intervention experiments, or independent expert annotations are needed to establish construct validity.

Several statistical tests appear to treat benchmark pairs as independent even though pairs share benchmarks and some reported entries are nested aggregates of the same benchmark family. The bootstrap procedure, uncertainty estimates, multiplicity correction, and exact sample counts are insufficiently specified; p-values are also reported as 0.00.

Important numerical and procedural inconsistencies undermine reproducibility: a claimed 1B-token corpus reportedly yields 8.45 billion token contexts; downsampling 8.45e9 by 1/50 would give 1.69e8 rather than the stated 1.69e7; and the stated complexity and feature counts are inconsistent across sections. The promised open-source link is incomplete in the manuscript.

The paper repeatedly moves from predictive association to claims about 'true overlap,' benchmark validity, and interconnected model capacities. Given the unresolved confounding, leakage, and lack of construct validation, these central interpretations are substantially stronger than the evidence supports.

strengths: The paper asks an important meta-evaluation question: whether proliferating LLM benchmarks measure distinct capabilities.
The proposed use of perplexity patterns from natural corpora is creative, and the study attempts broad coverage with 32 models, 89 benchmark/subtask columns, and both RedPajama and Dolma.
The appendix includes several useful sensitivity analyses involving alternative selectors, screening thresholds, corpus sizes, and held-out models.
The comparisons among semantic, performance, and signature-level relationships produce potentially interesting descriptive observations.
weaknesses: The central analysis is circular. Tokens are screened and selected specifically for their association with each benchmark's performance vector, and signature overlap is then computed from those same token-perplexity vectors over essentially the same models. Consequently, the claimed benchmark structure may be an artifact of supervised construction rather than independent evidence of shared capabilities.

The feature-selection regime is extremely prone to overfitting: roughly 32 observations are searched against millions of candidate features, followed by forward selection of about 30 predictors. AIC does not correct for the enormous adaptive search or post-selection inference, and highly correlated features will arise under the null.

The reported LOOCV does not clearly nest screening and feature selection inside every training fold. If signatures were selected using all models before cross-validation, the evaluation leaks held-out outcomes. The two-model experiment is also internally unclear: the paper starts with 32 models but says that 27 models were used after holding out two.

The validation evaluates prediction error, not whether the inferred pairwise overlaps or conclusions about capability structure generalize to independent models. No external ground truth establishes that signature correlation measures actual benchmark overlap, so interpretations such as coding being 'clean' or signatures resolving evaluation bias are unsupported.

Major confounds remain uncontrolled, including model size, architecture, model-family dependence, instruction tuning, tokenizer differences, and shared training data. Perplexity patterns and benchmark performance can both track these generic factors, while the cross-task experiment presented does not isolate them.

The semantic baseline is poorly constructed: entire question sets are concatenated and truncated to the embedding model's context limit. This discards most questions and is not a credible benchmark-level semantic-overlap measure, making the proposed method's apparent advantage over semantics difficult to interpret.

Several statistical analyses appear to treat dependent benchmark pairs as independent, and multiple testing is not adequately handled. Reported p-values of 0.00 and bootstrap significance therefore do not provide reliable inferential support.

The manuscript contains serious numerical and reproducibility inconsistencies. A claimed 1B-token corpus purportedly yields 8.45 billion contexts, and downsampling 8.45 billion by 1/50 would yield about 169 million rather than the reported 16.9 million. The released-resource claim is also incomplete in the manuscript text, which ends with 'in this' without a link.

The paper repeatedly moves from correlation to mechanistic or causal language—for example, claiming that signatures characterize capacity demands, filter noise, approximate true overlap, or reveal limited generalization—without interventions or adequate identification arguments.

Given the circular construction, high-dimensional selection bias, unclear leakage controls, and absence of independent validation for the main overlap claims, the central conclusions are not presently reliable despite the ambitious empirical effort.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely meta-evaluation problem: determining whether proliferating LLM benchmarks measure distinct capabilities.

The benchmark-signature idea is creative and potentially useful, moving beyond question embeddings and raw performance correlations by relating benchmark outcomes to perplexity patterns on natural corpora.
The empirical scope is substantial, covering 32 models, 89 reported benchmarks/subfields, and multiple capability categories.

The paper includes several valuable robustness checks, including alternative regularizers, screening methods, selection thresholds, corpus scales, a second corpus, leave-one-out prediction, and two held-out models.
The comparison among semantic-, performance-, and signature-level relationships yields interesting observations about benchmark-family and answer-format effects.
The presentation is generally clear, with helpful visualizations, algorithms, computational-cost reporting, and extensive appendices.
weaknesses: The central overlap analysis is statistically vulnerable to circularity. Tokens are selected for predicting each benchmark using the same 32-model performance vectors on which signature correlations are subsequently computed. Searching millions of features with only 32 observations can produce benchmark-tailored patterns even under weak or spurious associations. The reported prediction checks do not establish that the pairwise overlap matrices themselves generalize; signature discovery and overlap estimation should be separated using nested model-family-level splits or an independent model panel.

Forward AIC selection is poorly justified in this extreme d≫n regime. Signatures reportedly contain about 30 predictors for only 32 observations, making models nearly saturated, while ordinary AIC does not account for screening millions of candidates or post-selection uncertainty. No label-permutation or end-to-end null experiment is provided to quantify the structure that this pipeline creates by chance.

The 32 observations are not independent: many are size variants or checkpoints from the same model families. Shared architecture, scale, tokenizer, and post-training can jointly drive perplexity and benchmark scores. The two held-out models are too few, and appear related to families represented during training, so they do not adequately rule out family or scaling confounds.

The interpretation of signature correlation as capability overlap is not validated. Predictive association between corpus-token perplexity and benchmark scores can reflect model size, training mixture, tokenizer behavior, instruction tuning, or contamination rather than a shared capability. Claims that signatures approximate the 'true overlap,' resolve evaluation bias, or expose an LLM capacity space are consequently stronger than the evidence.

Perplexity features are not clearly comparable across heterogeneous tokenizers. A whitespace-delimited target may map to different subtoken sequences across models, and recording only the last token's perplexity can measure different events. Per-model z-scoring does not resolve this semantic mismatch.

The semantic baseline is weak: questions are concatenated and then truncated to the encoder limit, making similarity dependent largely on the beginning and ordering of a benchmark rather than its full item distribution. The equation and appendix algorithm also describe different bootstrap procedures. Thus the claim that signatures outperform semantic overlap is not convincing without stronger item-level embedding and matching baselines.

Several headline category conclusions rely on very sparse and uneven evidence. Coding, instruction following, and missing-information detection appear to be represented by individual benchmarks, while other categories contain many subfields; statements such as coding being uniquely 'clean' or isolated cannot be separated from dataset-specific effects.

Some robustness analyses assess stability rather than validity: agreement across regularizers, thresholds, corpus sizes, or two overlapping web corpora can show that a result is reproducible while leaving the same systematic confound intact. The random-feature baseline is sampled after correlation filtering and is therefore not a genuine null.

Reproducibility details contain notable inconsistencies. A claimed 1B-token source yields 8.45×10^9 contexts and then 1/50 downsampling is reported as 1.69×10^7 rather than 1.69×10^8; computational-complexity statements and the claimed 30–40 minute search over millions of AIC candidates are insufficiently reconciled with the stated algorithm. Prompting, few-shot settings, chat templates, seeds, uncertainty in benchmark scores, and an accessible code link are also not fully specified.

Overall, the proposal is promising and the study is ambitious, but the circular high-dimensional selection design and lack of an independent validation of the overlap matrix leave the central scientific claims insufficiently supported for acceptance at a top-tier venue.
